title: Chicxulub impact and the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction
summary: About 66.04 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide struck the shallow sea off Yucatán, triggering the mass extinction that ended the age of the dinosaurs.
card: An asteroid about 10 km across hit a carbonate-rich shallow sea at what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, leaving a buried crater some 180–200 km wide. Soot, dust and sulfur thrown into the atmosphere darkened and cooled the planet, and more than 60% of species died out within a geologically brief interval. The extinction marks the boundary between the Cretaceous and the Paleogene, and between the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras.
what:
Roughly 66.04 million years ago an asteroid struck the southern Gulf of Mexico, at a point now on the northern coast of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Modelling of the crater's buried structure indicates it came in from the northeast at a steep angle of about 45–60 degrees. It hit a sea floor built of carbonate and sulfate rock several kilometres thick, and within minutes excavated and collapsed into a multi-ring crater roughly 180–200 km across, with a central ring of peaks formed from uplifted basement rock capped by melt rock. Seawater surged back into the crater within the hour, and a tsunami reflected from the rim reached the centre within about a day, leaving sand, gravel and charcoal from burning forests.

Ejecta spread across the whole planet. Near the crater it forms breccias tens to hundreds of metres thick; around the Gulf it includes tsunami and slump deposits; far away it is a thin clay layer rich in iridium, shocked quartz and glass spherules. Soot, rock dust and an estimated 100–500 gigatonnes of sulfur lofted into the atmosphere blocked sunlight and cooled the climate, collapsing photosynthesis on land and in the oceans. More than 60% of Cretaceous species disappeared, among them the non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, marine reptiles, ammonites and many groups of marine plankton.

Argon dating places the K–Pg boundary at about 66.043 million years ago and shows the impact and the extinction coincide within about 32,000 years; older publications give 65.0 or 65.5 million years because of earlier calibrations. Scientists agree the impact happened at the boundary; a minority still argues that the Deccan Traps eruptions in India were the main driver of the extinction, while most recent studies find the impact alone coincides with the extinction pulse.

The crater is buried beneath younger sediments. It was identified in 1991 from gravity and magnetic anomalies and oil-well cores, and was later cored through its peak ring by IODP–ICDP Expedition 364.

uncertainty.note: Impact age ±0.010–0.011 Ma is analytical (1σ); a different Fish Canyon sanidine standard age could shift 40Ar/39Ar dates by up to ~200 kyr (Schoene et al. 2021). The end bound is the upper limit of impact–extinction synchrony (within 32 kyr, Renne et al. 2013), not a measured extinction duration.

how: The impactor, estimated at about 10 km in diameter, struck at a steep angle (about 45–60°) from the northeast into a 3–4 km thick sequence of carbonate and sulfate-bearing sedimentary rock. The transient crater was about 100 km wide; within minutes its uplifted centre collapsed outward to form a peak ring, giving a final crater of about 180–200 km. Earthquakes far stronger than any recorded today, Gulf-wide tsunamis and slumping followed. Ejecta, some of it thrown out at several kilometres per second, rained back worldwide as spherules, shocked quartz and an iridium-rich clay; re-entering ejecta may have heated the atmosphere and ignited wildfires, as charcoal in the crater infill suggests. The vaporised target released an estimated 100–500 Gt of sulfur, which formed sunlight-absorbing aerosols, along with soot and dust. The resulting darkness and cooling suppressed photosynthesis, collapsing food chains from plankton upward; a sharp carbon-isotope excursion records the disruption of the carbon cycle, whose atmospheric part probably recovered in under about 5,000 years.
why_it_matters:
The Chicxulub impact closed the Mesozoic Era. By removing the non-avian dinosaurs and many marine groups, it emptied ecological roles that surviving lineages, including the mammals, filled during the Paleogene; the modern dominance of mammals, and so the eventual evolution of primates and humans, sits downstream of that turnover. Had the asteroid missed, or struck deep ocean crust rather than a sulfur- and carbonate-rich shelf, the climatic shock would likely have been very different, and the dinosaur-dominated ecosystems of the late Cretaceous might have persisted.

The event also changed science. The 1980 discovery of an iridium spike in boundary clay launched the impact hypothesis; locating the crater in 1991 turned a controversial idea into one of the best-tested causal explanations in Earth history, and showed that sudden external catastrophes, not only slow change, shape life's history. Its details mattered too: modelling suggests that a steep impact like this one releases more climate-changing gas per unit of impactor mass than a grazing or vertical strike would have. The boundary layer it laid down is the global marker geologists use to define the start of the Cenozoic.

perspectives.holder: Majority view: Schulte et al. 2010 (41-author review) and later work
perspectives.account: A single ejecta layer chemically tied to Chicxulub lies exactly at the extinction horizon worldwide, and fossil patterns match modelled darkness and cooling, so the impact triggered the mass extinction; Deccan volcanism contributed environmental stress at most.

perspectives.holder: Minority view associated with G. Keller and colleagues; Deccan timing studies
perspectives.account: Deccan Traps flood basalts erupted in large pulses during the same ~700–800 kyr window, one pulse beginning before the impact, so volcanism may have been a major or even primary driver; the relative timing of eruption pulses and impact is still debated between U–Pb and 40Ar/39Ar datasets.
